nameStory: The "three-square" part of this bulrush's name comes from its distinctive triangular stems that feel sharply three-sided when you roll them between your fingers. "Chairmaker's bulrush" reflects its traditional use - Native Americans and early settlers wove the tough, flexible stems into chair seats and baskets. The "American" in its scientific name honors its New World origins.
description: American three-square bulrush is a tall, grass-like wetland plant that grows in dense clumps along saltwater and brackish shores. It reaches 2-4 feet tall with distinctive triangular stems that feel sharp-edged to the touch. The plant produces small, brownish flower clusters near the top of its stems and has long, narrow leaves that emerge from the base. It's a member of the sedge family, not a true grass, though it might fool you at first glance.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Distinctly triangular in cross-section with sharp edges you can feel when rolling between your fingers - this three-sided shape gives the plant its name

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small brown to reddish-brown flower clusters (called spikelets) appear near the stem tips, looking like tiny bristly footballs clustered together

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Long, narrow, grass-like leaves emerge from the base of the plant and are often shorter than the flowering stems

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms dense colonies or clumps, spreading by underground rhizomes to create patches that sway together in the wind

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Stems feel firm and rigid, tough enough to weave with, unlike softer grasses that bend easily

habitat: Look for American three-square bulrush along salt marshes, brackish ponds, and tidal areas throughout coastal New England. It thrives in wet, salty soils where few other plants can survive, often growing alongside cordgrass and other salt-tolerant species. You'll find it in the zone where saltwater regularly floods the ground.

seasonality.spring: New green shoots emerge from the base, and the distinctive triangular stems become apparent as they grow taller.
seasonality.summer: Peak flowering period with brown spikelets developing at stem tips, and plants reach full height in dense, swaying colonies.
seasonality.fall: Flower clusters mature and release seeds, while stems begin to turn golden-brown but remain standing.
seasonality.winter: Dead stems persist through winter, still showing the diagnostic triangular shape and providing structure in the marsh landscape.

funFact: This bulrush is so salt-tolerant that it can actually excrete salt crystals through special glands on its leaves - on sunny days after high tide, you might see tiny white salt deposits sparkling on the plant like natural glitter!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other bulrushes and sedges, but the sharply triangular stem is your best clue - remember "sedges have edges" and this one has three very distinct ones. True grasses have round, hollow stems, while this sedge's stem is solid and triangular.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its common name including "bulrush," this plant is actually a sedge, not a rush - botanical naming can be confusing! The old basket-making tradition gives it historical importance, as Native American communities used it extensively for weaving waterproof containers and mats.
compareHints: American three-square bulrush is distinguished from its bulrush relatives by its sharply triangular stems and salt-tolerant habitat. Three-square bulrush (S. pungens) is very similar but typically smaller, while soft-stemmed bulrush has round, soft stems you can squeeze. The coastal, salty habitat is also a key difference from most other bulrushes that prefer freshwater.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its bulrush relatives, three-square is the only one with the distinctive triangular stem - soft-stemmed bulrush has round, squishy stems, while hardstem bulrush has round, firm stems.

Water bulrush stands apart from other bulrushes by its aquatic lifestyle and incredibly thin stems.
Among New England's bulrushes, hardstem bulrush is distinguished by its exceptional height and remarkably rigid stems.
Among New England bulrushes, Torrey's is distinguished by its moderate triangular stems that aren't as sharply angled as three-square bulrush or as round as soft-stemmed bulrush.

Among its bulrush relatives, slender bulrush stands out for its perfectly cylindrical stems - three-square bulrush and American three-square bulrush both have distinctly triangular stems you can feel with your fingers.
Common club-rush stands out from other New England bulrushes by having perfectly round, completely leafless stems.
